examples.title: Check whether a function is a valid probability function
examples.prompt: Which of these functions could be probability functions of a discrete random variable \(X\)? Each is 0 elsewhere.

steps.say: Every value of f2, f4 and f5 is between 0 and 1. The function f3 gives a negative value at x of 3, so f3 already fails.
The sums are 1.1 for f2, 1.0 for f3, 0.9 for f4 and 1 for f5. So f3 adds to 1 even though one of its values is negative.
Only f5 is a probability function. f2 breaks the sum rule because it totals 1.1, f4 breaks it because it totals 0.9, and f3 breaks the rule that no probability is negative.

examples.title: Turn a CDF graph into a probability function
examples.prompt: The d.f. \(F(y)\) of the discrete random variable \(Y\) is a staircase. It is 0 for \(y<-2\), \(\tfrac{1}{3}\) for \(-2\le y<1\), \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) for \(1\le y<3\) and 1 for \(y\ge 3\). Write \(f(y)\) for all values of \(y\).

steps.say: The staircase jumps at y of minus 2, at y of 1 and at y of 3, so those are the only values Y can take.
Each jump is the new height minus the old height, so the jumps are one third, one sixth and one half.
Each value is written next to its jump size.
work: f(y)=\tfrac{1}{3} \text{ for } y=-2,\quad \tfrac{1}{6} \text{ for } y=1,\quad \tfrac{1}{2} \text{ for } y=3

steps.say: Every other value of y gets probability 0, so the function is now defined for all y.
The three probabilities add to 1, so f is a valid probability function.

examples.title: Read a probability from the CDF
examples.prompt: For the same \(Y\) (jumps of \(\tfrac{1}{3}\) at \(-2\), \(\tfrac{1}{6}\) at 1 and \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) at 3), find (ii) \(P(Y>-1)\) and (iii) \(P(-0.5<Y<2.25)\).

steps.say: Both questions are rewritten with less than or equal to, so they can be read from F.
F at minus 1 is one third because only the jump at minus 2 has been collected, so the right tail is two thirds.
F at 2.25 is one half and F at minus 0.5 is one third, so the interval holds one sixth.
None of minus 1, minus 0.5 or 2.25 is a value Y can take, so strict or not strict gives the same answer here. Adding the jumps at 1 and 3 confirms two thirds.

examples.title: Expected value and variance of a discrete variable

steps.say: The four values are paired with their probabilities, and the probabilities add to 1.
Each value times its probability gives minus 0.55, 0.3, 0.3 and 1.4, so the expected value is 1.45.
The weighted squared distances from 1.45 add to 9.7475. The shortcut with E of X squared, which is 11.85, gives the same variance.
The SD is the square root of 9.7475, so X spreads about 3.122 units around its mean of 1.45.
